body: What this converter does

Kruti Dev is not an encoding. It is a font whose glyphs happen to sit on ASCII codepoints, which is why a Kruti Dev document opened on a machine without the font shows up as gibberish like Hkkjr instead of भारत. Converting it to Unicode is not a matter of swapping one letter for another. The characters have to be reordered, because the two systems store Hindi differently.

This page does that reordering properly. Type or paste on the left and the Unicode output appears on the right as you type. There is no Convert button to hunt for, no advertisement between you and the text box, and no upload.
Why the output may look different from other converters
Two things go wrong in most Kruti Dev converters, and both are easy to miss because the broken output still looks like Hindi:

• The short-i matra. In Kruti Dev you type the ि before the consonant, because that is where it is drawn. Unicode wants it after. If a converter copies the visual order straight across, you get text that renders acceptably in some fonts but fails search, sorting, spell-check and screen readers.
  • The reph. The र् that rides above a letter is typed after its syllable in Kruti Dev, so कर्म is keyed as deZ. It has to be moved to the front of the cluster, and it has to be moved before the i-matra is repositioned, or words like कीर्ति come out scrambled.
Split vowel signs are handled too: Kruti Dev builds ो out of an aa-matra plus an e-matra, so dks has to be recomposed into को rather than left as two separate marks.
Who needs this

Government offices across India still run on Kruti Dev. Court orders, file notings, tender documents, school records and exam papers were typed in it for two decades. But portals, databases and e-governance systems all expect Unicode, so every time an old document has to go into a new system, somebody has to convert it. Typists preparing for CPCT, RSCIT and state stenography exams need the reverse direction just as often.
How to use it

1. Open your Kruti Dev document and copy the Hindi text.
  2. Paste it into the left panel. The output appears immediately.
  3. Press Copy text, or Download .docx to get a Word file with the correct font already applied.
  4. Read the output before you use it. Very old documents sometimes carry unusual characters, and this is the one place where it is worth a glance.
If you need the other direction, the Unicode to Kruti Dev converter does the same work in reverse, and Kruti Dev to Mangal shows the result in the Mangal font that most government forms ask for.

faq.q: Is this Kruti Dev to Unicode converter free?
faq.a: Yes, completely. There is no signup, no character limit and no paid tier. The converter is a static web page, so there is nothing to charge for.

faq.q: Does my text get uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. The entire conversion engine is JavaScript that runs inside your browser. Nothing is sent to a server, which means you can convert confidential file notings and draft orders without them leaving your machine. You can disconnect from the internet after the page loads and it will still work.

faq.q: Why does the i-matra (ि) come out in a different place than in my Kruti Dev file?
faq.a: Because that is correct. Kruti Dev stores glyphs in visual order, so the short-i sign is typed before its consonant. Unicode stores them in logical order, where the sign belongs after the consonant. So fd becomes कि, not ि followed by क. Converters that skip this step produce text that looks right but breaks search, sorting and spell-check.

faq.q: What about conjuncts like क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ and श्र?
faq.a: They are mapped explicitly, along with the reph (र्), the rakar (्र), half letters and nukta characters. The reph is the other common failure: in Kruti Dev it is typed after the syllable it sits on, so कर्म is keyed as deZ and has to be moved back into place.

faq.q: Will my English words and numbers be converted too?
faq.a: Dates, numbers, percentages, URLs and email addresses are always left untouched. Common English words are detected and preserved as well. Because a legacy font stores Hindi as plain ASCII, an unusual proper noun can still be converted by mistake. You can turn the whole behaviour off with the checkbox under the panels.

faq.q: Is Kruti Dev the same as Mangal?
faq.a: No, and this trips a lot of people up. Kruti Dev is a legacy font that maps Hindi letters onto ASCII slots. Mangal is a Unicode font that ships with Windows. So "Kruti Dev to Mangal" really means "Kruti Dev to Unicode, displayed in Mangal". See the Kruti Dev to Mangal converter.

faq.q: Can I convert back to Kruti Dev?
faq.a: Yes. Each page converts in one fixed direction, so for the reverse use the Unicode to Kruti Dev converter. There is a link to it under the boxes as well. That page also accepts Hindi typed straight from a phone or Windows keypad, since keypad Hindi is already Unicode.

body: “Hindi to Kruti Dev” is this page

If you type Hindi on an Android or iPhone keypad, or with the Windows Hindi keyboard, or paste it from WhatsApp or a website, that text is already Unicode. There is no separate “Hindi” format to convert from. So this one page covers both “Hindi to Kruti Dev” and “Unicode to Kruti Dev”. They are the same conversion.
The same goes for Mangal and Nirmala UI: both are Unicode fonts, so text in either of them can be pasted straight into the box on the left.
Unicode to Kruti Dev, the right way round

Converting into a legacy font is harder than converting out of one, because the text has to be put back into visual order. Every short-i matra has to move to the front of its consonant cluster, every reph has to move to the end of the syllable it belongs to, and the composed vowel signs ो, ौ and ॉ have to be split back into the two glyphs Kruti Dev draws them with.
This page does all of that as you type. The output is plain ASCII, which is what Kruti Dev text is, and it turns into Hindi the moment the Kruti Dev font is applied to it.
What to do with the output

1. Copy the right-hand panel, or use Download .docx.
  2. Paste into Word, LibreOffice or your DTP application.
  3. Select the pasted text and set the font to Kruti Dev 010. The .docx download does this step for you.
If the text still looks like English letters after that, the font is not installed on that machine. See Kruti Dev font download.
Who uses this direction

Printing presses and DTP shops that have twenty years of Kruti Dev templates. Candidates practising for CPCT, RSCIT and state stenography tests, which are still conducted in Kruti Dev. Offices that receive a Unicode draft from one department and have to fit it into a legacy template from another. And anyone maintaining an old publication where switching the whole archive to Unicode is not realistic.
A note on exact spellings

Kruti Dev often offers more than one way to key the same letter. Where that happens the converter picks a single canonical spelling, so its output may not be byte-identical to text a person typed by hand. It renders identically, and converting it back with the Kruti Dev to Unicode converter returns exactly what you started with.

faq.q: I want to convert Hindi to Kruti Dev. Is this the right page?
faq.a: Yes. Hindi typed on a phone keypad, the Windows Hindi keyboard, or copied from a website or WhatsApp is already Unicode. "Hindi" and "Unicode" mean the same thing here, so "Hindi to Kruti Dev" and "Unicode to Kruti Dev" are one page. Paste it into the left box and you will get Kruti Dev on the right.

faq.a: Yes. Switch your keyboard to Hindi and type into the left box, which is set up for Devanagari input. Typing Hindi phonetically in English letters ("namaste" for नमस्ते) is not supported yet; that is a separate feature called transliteration.

faq.q: Why would I convert Unicode back to Kruti Dev?
faq.a: Three common reasons: a printing press or DTP operator still works in Kruti Dev and needs the file in that font; a typing test or stenography exam is conducted in Kruti Dev and you want practice material; or an old template has to stay consistent with documents typed years ago.

faq.q: The output looks like random English letters. Is that a bug?
faq.a: No, that is exactly what Kruti Dev text is. It only becomes Hindi when the Kruti Dev font is applied to it. Paste the output into Word, select it, and set the font to Kruti Dev 010, or use the Download .docx button, which applies the font for you.

faq.q: Do I need the Kruti Dev font installed to use this page?
faq.a: Not to convert. You only need the font to see the result as Hindi. Without it the output panel shows the underlying ASCII, which is still correct and still pastes correctly into any application that has the font.

faq.q: Will the result be identical to text originally typed in Kruti Dev?
faq.a: It will be equivalent, but not always character-for-character identical. Several Kruti Dev key sequences produce the same letter (क can be keyed two different ways), so the converter picks one canonical spelling. Converting back to Unicode returns the original text either way.

faq.q: What happens to English words and numbers?
faq.a: They are left alone by default, which matters more in this direction than the other: converting the digits in a date or an account number would silently corrupt it. You can switch the behaviour off with the checkbox under the panels.

faq.q: Does it handle half letters and conjuncts?
faq.a: Yes. Half consonants, the reph, the rakar, nukta letters and the ligatures क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ and श्र are all mapped, and the i-matra is moved back to the front of its cluster where Kruti Dev expects it.

body: First, the thing nobody tells you

Mangal is a font, not an encoding. It is the Unicode Devanagari font that Microsoft has shipped with Windows since XP. Kruti Dev, by contrast, is a legacy font that maps Hindi onto ASCII slots, which is why a Kruti Dev document looks like Hkkjr on a computer that does not have it.

So "Kruti Dev to Mangal" is really "Kruti Dev to Unicode, shown in Mangal". The text this page gives you is standard Unicode Hindi. Paste it into a form, a portal, an email or a database and it will be correct regardless of which Devanagari font ends up rendering it.
Why your department asks for Mangal

When Unicode Hindi first became practical in government work, Mangal was the only Devanagari font you could rely on being installed on every Windows machine. Specifying it in a circular was a way of guaranteeing that a form would look the same in every office. That instruction has outlived its reason, because Nirmala UI and Noto Sans Devanagari render the same text just as well, but the wording survives in departmental guidance, which is why people search for "Kruti Dev to Mangal" rather than "to Unicode".

If a portal rejects your text, the problem is almost never the font. It is usually that the text was pasted as Kruti Dev ASCII rather than converted, or that the matra order is wrong, which is precisely what this converter fixes.
Getting it into a document as Mangal

1. Paste your Kruti Dev text on the left. The Mangal output appears as you type.
  2. Press Download .docx for a Word file with Mangal already applied, or Copy text to paste it yourself.
  3. If you paste manually into Word, select the text and pick Mangal from the font list. Setting the font does not change the characters, it only changes how they are drawn.
Mangal, Nirmala UI or Noto?

Mangal is the oldest and has the most conservative letterforms, which is why it still reads as the "official" choice. Nirmala UI, introduced with Windows 8, is cleaner on screen. Noto Sans Devanagari is Google's open font and is what this site uses for its own Hindi text. All three display identical Unicode, so pick whichever your form asks for, and do not worry that the underlying text changes. It does not.
Need plain Unicode without the Mangal framing? Use the Kruti Dev to Unicode converter. Going the other way? Try Mangal to Kruti Dev.

faq.q: Is Mangal a different encoding from Unicode?
faq.a: No, and this is the single most useful thing to know here. Mangal is a font, not an encoding. It is an OpenType Unicode font that Microsoft ships with Windows. So "Kruti Dev to Mangal" means "Kruti Dev to Unicode, then displayed in Mangal". The text this page produces is ordinary Unicode Hindi and will work in any Unicode font.

faq.q: Why do government forms specifically ask for Mangal?
faq.a: Because Mangal was the first Devanagari font guaranteed to be present on every Windows machine, so specifying it meant a form would render the same way in every office. Many departmental circulars still name it by habit. In practice any Unicode Devanagari font (Mangal, Nirmala UI, Noto Sans Devanagari) displays the same characters.

faq.q: The output panel does not look like Mangal on my device.
faq.a: The panel asks for Mangal first and falls back to another Devanagari font if it is not installed, which is normal on Mac, Linux, Android and iOS, where Mangal does not ship. The characters are identical either way. On Windows it will render in genuine Mangal.

faq.q: How do I get the converted text into a Word file as Mangal?
faq.a: Use the Download .docx button. The file is written with Mangal already applied to every paragraph. Or copy the text, paste it into Word, select it and choose Mangal from the font list.

faq.q: Is the matra order handled correctly?
faq.a: Yes. The short-i sign is moved after its consonant, the reph is moved to the front of its cluster, split vowel signs are recomposed and the conjuncts क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ and श्र are mapped explicitly. This is the part most converters get wrong, and it is why text from elsewhere sometimes fails search or spell-check even though it looks fine.

faq.a: Yes. See the Mangal to Kruti Dev converter. There is a link to it under the boxes on this page too.

Most people who need to write a line of Hindi do not have a Hindi keyboard set up, and do not want to install one for a single WhatsApp message or form field. This page solves that: you type namaste and get नमस्ते, you type mera naam ram hai and get मेरा नाम राम है. The English letters are read as sounds and written back out in Devanagari.

The output is ordinary Unicode Hindi, so it works everywhere - WhatsApp, email, Word, government portals, social media, search. If you need the legacy Kruti Dev font instead, paste the result into the Unicode to Kruti Dev converter.
Transliteration is not translation

This is the one thing worth being clear about before you use it. The page changes the script, not the language. Type computer and you get कंप्यूटर - the English word written in Devanagari - not the Hindi word for a computer. That is almost always what people want when they are typing a message, because the sentence they have in their head is already Hindi; they just cannot type the letters.
Spelling rules worth knowing
You do not need to learn a system. Type the word as it sounds and it will usually be right. These few patterns cover the letters English has no spelling for:

• Aspirated consonants add an h. kh ख, gh घ, ch च, chh छ, th थ, dh ध, ph फ, bh भ, sh श.
  • Long vowels double. aa आ, ee or ii ई, oo or uu ऊ. So kitab and kitaab both give किताब, but doubling is the way to be sure.
  • Conjuncts have short spellings. ksh क्ष, tra त्र, gya ज्ञ, shr श्र, and ri for ऋ.
  • Nasals look after themselves. An n or m before another consonant becomes the anusvara, so hindi gives हिंदी and mandir gives मंदिर.
Where it guesses, and what to do about it

English spelling throws away information Hindi needs. One a has to stand for both अ and आ, so bharat could be भारत or भरत and the letters alone cannot say which. Hindi also drops the final vowel that Devanagari still writes, which is why ghar has to become घर and not घर्.

Two things handle it. As you type, each word is looked up in Google's Hindi input service - the same transliteration behind Gboard - and its top suggestion is used, which gets the long tail right: thela becomes ठेला, tokar becomes टोकर. If that service cannot be reached, a built-in dictionary of common words plus a set of spelling rules takes over automatically, and the page tells you it has. When a word still comes out wrong, spell the long vowel out (bhaarat, suuraj) and it will fix itself.

For anything that has to be right first time - a name, a legal document, Sanskrit - switch Typing to Exact (ITRANS). That mode does no guessing at all: aa ii uu are the long vowels, capital T D N S are the retroflex consonants, .n is the anusvara and .N the chandrabindu. What you write is exactly what you get.
Where this fits with the rest of the site

The other pages here convert between Hindi fonts - they take text that already exists and move it between Kruti Dev, DevLys, Mangal and Unicode. That is an exact mapping with a right answer. This page is the other problem: you have no Hindi text yet, and you need to produce some. It is a separate tool with a separate engine, because a guess and a conversion should never be mistaken for each other.

If you already have a file in a legacy font, you want Kruti Dev to Unicode or DevLys to Unicode instead. If you have Hindi and need it in a legacy font, that is Unicode to Kruti Dev. The full list has the rest.

body: A tutor, not just a test

Most Hindi typing pages hand you a paragraph and a clock. That measures where you are; it does not move you. This one teaches the layout: the key you need next is lit on the keyboard, the finger that should press it is coloured on the hands, and the passage marks every akshara green or red as you go. When a letter needs Shift, it also shows which little finger should be holding it.

What the tutor checks underneath is the Kruti Dev keystrokes that produce it, worked out by the same conversion engine that powers the converters on this site - so what you read and what you press are guaranteed to be the same sentence.
Remington or InScript
This is the first thing to get right, because they are different keyboards and practising the wrong one is wasted effort.

• Remington (Kruti Dev, DevLys) puts Hindi letters on the English key positions. CPCT, SSC, high court and district court recruitment and many state posts still set their Hindi typing paper this way. If your notification names a font, it is this one.
  • InScript (Mangal, Unicode) is the layout built into Windows, used for modern office work, portals and anything that ends up on a website. It has its own key arrangement and its own muscle memory.

This tutor teaches Remington. If you need InScript, turn on the Windows Hindi keypad and practise with that instead - and if you only need to write a line of Hindi rather than build speed, the on-screen Hindi keyboard or English to Hindi typing will get you there faster.
The lessons

Eleven levels. The first five each open one more row. Level 1 is the home row alone - क, स, र, ह, य and four matras, all typed without moving a finger off its resting key. Then the top row, the bottom row, numbers, and Shift.

Once every key is reachable the levels stop being about rows and start being about the script. Level 6 is the matras - ि ी ु ू े ै ो ौ - on consonants you already know, so the only new thing on screen is the vowel sign and the rule that ि is typed before its letter. Level 7 drills the letters with no key of their own - भ, श, ष, ण, ध, ख, घ, झ, थ - which are two keystrokes each and are where most Kruti Dev typists quietly lose their speed. Level 8 is the four conjuncts क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ and श्र, which look like new letters and are not: they are built from letters you have, with the halant you already use. Levels 9 to 11 are everyday words, sentences and finally paragraphs.
A level unlocks the next when you type the whole drill at its accuracy target. Speed is recorded but never required, because gating on speed teaches you to rush a drill you have not learned yet.
Getting faster

1. Slow down until you are clean. Type at whatever pace holds you above 95% accuracy, even if it feels absurdly slow. Speed follows; corrected habits do not.
  2. Stop looking at your hands. Use the on-screen keyboard instead - that is what it is for. Every glance down costs you your place and resets your rhythm.
  3. Drill the awkward letters on purpose. The two-key consonants and the ि matra, which is typed before its consonant, are worth more practice than the rest of the alphabet combined.
  4. Little and often. Twenty minutes daily beats three hours on a Sunday: muscle memory consolidates between sessions rather than during them.
  5. Sit the full length. A 30-minute test is a different skill from a 1-minute burst, and stamina is the part nobody practises. Work up through the lengths rather than always taking the short one - the tests here run to two hours for exactly that reason, and the clock pauses if you need to stop.

Most people who need a line of Hindi do not have a Hindi keypad set up and are not about to install one for a single form field, a WhatsApp message or a name that has to be written correctly. That is what this page is for. The letters are on screen, you click them, and the Hindi builds up in the box above. When you are finished you copy it and paste it wherever it was going.

The output is ordinary Unicode Devanagari, which is what every modern system expects - government portals, email, Word, search, social media, databases. If you specifically need the legacy font instead, paste it into the Unicode to Kruti Dev converter.
How the letters are arranged

In वर्णमाला order, the order every Hindi speaker learned at school: the vowels, then the consonants in their five groups (with the halant, anusvara, chandrabindu and visarga beside them), then the everyday conjuncts, then digits. Space, Backspace, Enter and the full stop । are on the bottom row.

This is deliberately not an InScript picture. InScript scatters Devanagari across the QWERTY key positions, which is exactly right if you have learned the layout and are looking for the physical key - and exactly wrong if you are finding each letter by eye, because the letters end up in no order at all. Anyone who does know InScript has it installed already and can simply type; this page is for everyone else.
Matras, half letters and conjuncts
Three things cover almost everything people get stuck on:

• Vowels turn into matras after a consonant. Click क, then इ, and you get कि - even though the sign is drawn to the left of the letter. The vowel keys show the matra they will type, so there is no separate matra row to hunt through.
  • The halant makes a half letter. ◌् after a consonant silences its vowel, so क + ् + य is क्य. That is how every conjunct is built.
  • The common conjuncts have their own keys. क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ and श्र turn up constantly, so they are one click rather than three.

The dotted circles on the sign keys are not characters. A vowel sign has no shape of its own, so the circle stands in for the consonant it will attach to - the same convention the Unicode charts use. Only the sign itself is inserted.
Second layer

More letters opens the rest: the Sanskrit vowels (ॠ ऌ ॡ), the candra signs English loanwords use (ऑ in डॉक्टर), the Marathi and southern letters, the nukta, and the remaining punctuation. None of it is needed for ordinary Hindi, which is why it is behind a toggle rather than on the first screen.

body: What this converter does

DevLys is not an encoding. It is a font whose glyphs sit on ASCII codepoints, which is why a DevLys document opened on a machine without the font shows gibberish like Hkkjr instead of भारत. Turning it into Unicode is not a matter of swapping one letter for another - the characters have to be reordered, because the two systems store Hindi differently.
Paste on the left and the Unicode appears on the right as you type. No Convert button to hunt for, no advertisement between you and the text box, and no upload.
DevLys and Kruti Dev: close, and checked

DevLys 010 and Kruti Dev 010 share a keyboard layout. That is genuinely useful - it means two decades of Hindi DTP work is interchangeable at the keystroke level - but it is also the assumption that quietly breaks most converters, because the two fonts are not identical everywhere.

So it was verified rather than assumed. Every character code this converter uses was read out of both font files and compared: advance width, contour count and bounding box. All of them match. The two fonts do diverge in one block of character codes, and the conversion table deliberately does not use any code in that block. That is why this page is live and why the Chanakya pages are not.
What usually goes wrong elsewhere

• The short-i matra. In DevLys you type the ि before its consonant, because that is where it is drawn. Unicode wants it after. Copy the visual order straight across and you get text that renders acceptably in some fonts but fails search, sorting, spell-check and screen readers.
  • The reph. The र् that rides above a letter is typed after its syllable, so कर्म is keyed as deZ. It has to be moved to the front of the cluster, and moved before the i-matra is repositioned, or words like कीर्ति come out scrambled.
  • Split vowel signs. DevLys builds ो from an aa-matra plus an e-matra, so dks has to be recomposed into को rather than left as two marks.
Who needs this

DevLys turns up wherever Hindi DTP was done in the 1990s and 2000s: press and publishing files, school and college records, tender documents, old court and municipal paperwork. Modern portals, databases and e-governance systems all expect Unicode, so every time one of those files has to go into a new system, somebody has to convert it.
How to use it

1. Open your DevLys document and copy the Hindi text.
  2. Paste it into the left panel. The output appears immediately.
  3. Press Copy text, or Download .docx for a Word file with the correct font already applied.
  4. Read the output before you use it. Very old documents sometimes carry unusual characters, and this is the one place a glance pays for itself.

For the other direction use Unicode to DevLys, and DevLys to Mangal shows the result in the Mangal font most government forms ask for. If your document is actually Kruti Dev, Kruti Dev to Unicode is the page you want.

faq.a: They are different fonts that share a keyboard layout. Every key this converter uses draws the same Hindi letter in both - that was checked by comparing the two font files glyph by glyph, not assumed. So a DevLys document and a Kruti Dev document containing the same keystrokes hold the same Hindi, even though the letterforms on screen differ slightly.

faq.a: Because "almost the same" is not good enough for a converter. The two fonts genuinely do differ in one block of character codes. The page went live only once it was confirmed that the conversion table never touches that block, so the overlap it relies on is real rather than approximate.

So fd becomes कि. Converters that skip this step produce text that looks right but breaks search, sorting and spell-check.

This is the direction you need when a document has to go back into a legacy workflow: a press file, a school register, a form that was laid out in DevLys years ago and still has to match. You type Hindi the modern way - phone keypad, Windows Hindi keyboard, or pasted from anywhere on the web - and get DevLys keystrokes out.

The output will look like nonsense Latin text, and that is correct. DevLys stores Hindi as ASCII and relies on the font to draw the letters. Paste it into Word, select it, apply DevLys 010, and it reads as Hindi.

body: Which converter do you need?

The converter above is the one most people arrive looking for: paste Kruti Dev, get Unicode Hindi you can use anywhere. If that is not your direction, every conversion has its own page, so you pick the conversion by picking the page rather than wrestling with a dropdown.

• Kruti Dev to Unicode: an old Word file into Hindi that works on the web, in WhatsApp and on government portals.
  • Unicode to Kruti Dev: Hindi you typed on a keypad back into Kruti Dev keys, for a form or template that still demands the legacy font.
  • Kruti Dev to Mangal: the same Unicode output, labelled for people whose documents are set in Mangal.
  • Mangal to Kruti Dev: the reverse.
  • All converters: the full list, including the ones still being verified.
Hindi, Unicode and Mangal are the same thing

Text typed on a phone or on the Windows Hindi keypad is already Unicode. The characters are real Devanagari: न is stored as the letter न, and any font can draw it. Mangal is simply one such font, shipped with Windows. So "Hindi", "Unicode" and "Mangal" describe one kind of text with three names, and this site labels the boxes "Unicode / Hindi" so both audiences recognise their own word.
That is also why there is no separate "Hindi to Mangal" page. There would be nothing for it to do.
Kruti Dev and DevLys are not Hindi

A legacy font works the other way round. Kruti Dev does not store Devanagari at all. It stores ordinary English letters and punctuation, and the font file draws a Hindi glyph in place of each one. The word नमो is stored as the four characters ueksS.
Two consequences follow, and between them they explain almost every problem people bring to a converter:

• Without the font, the text is unreadable. Send a Kruti Dev document to someone who does not have Kruti Dev installed and they see the raw keystrokes. Paste it into a website and it stays gibberish forever, because a web page cannot borrow a font from your hard disk.
  • Nothing can search or spell-check it. To a computer it is English nonsense. Search, sorting, screen readers and translation all fail.
Converting to Unicode fixes both permanently. That is the direction worth taking if you have a choice.
Working out which font an old document used

Open the file and look at the font name in the toolbar. That is usually the fastest answer. If the file has lost its formatting, the keystrokes themselves are a clue: Kruti Dev and DevLys 010 share almost the same layout, so fgUnh reading as हिन्दी points at one of those two. Chanakya and Shusha use genuinely different layouts and will not decode correctly with a Kruti Dev map, which is why their pages stay marked coming soon rather than returning plausible-looking rubbish.
If the text already looks like Hindi on a machine with no special fonts installed, it is Unicode and needs no conversion at all.

faq.q: Which Hindi font converter do I actually need?
faq.a: Work backwards from where the text is going. Going into a website, WhatsApp, email or a government portal, you need Unicode, so use Kruti Dev to Unicode. Going into an old Word template or a form that must stay in Kruti Dev, you need the legacy keys, so use Unicode to Kruti Dev.

faq.q: Is Hindi the same as Unicode?
faq.a: For this site, yes. Anything typed on a phone or on the Windows Hindi keypad is already Unicode Hindi. The two words describe the same text, which is why the boxes are labelled "Unicode / Hindi". Kruti Dev and DevLys are the exception: they are not Hindi at all, they are English keystrokes that a font draws as Hindi.

faq.q: Why does my Kruti Dev text look like gibberish?
faq.a: Because it is. A Kruti Dev document stores ueksS, not नमो. The Hindi only appears when the Kruti Dev font is installed and applied. Open the same file on a machine without the font and you see the raw keystrokes. That is normal, and it is exactly what this converter translates.

faq.q: What is the difference between Mangal and Unicode?
faq.a: None, at the level that matters. Mangal is a Unicode font: a Mangal document already contains real Devanagari characters. Converting "Kruti Dev to Mangal" and "Kruti Dev to Unicode" produces the same characters. The only difference is which font your document is set to display them in.

faq.q: Do Kruti Dev and DevLys use the same keyboard?
faq.a: Almost. DevLys 010 and Kruti Dev 010 share nearly the whole layout, which is why DevLys is offered as a preview font on the Kruti Dev pages. "Almost" is not "exactly", though, so the DevLys converters stay marked coming soon until the differences have been checked against real DevLys documents.

faq.q: Is my text uploaded anywhere?
faq.a: No. Every converter on this site runs entirely in your browser. Nothing you paste is sent to a server, logged or stored. You can disconnect from the internet after the page loads and it still works.

body: What this is

A Hindi legacy-font converter that tries to get the hard parts right: the short-i matra that sits on the wrong side of its consonant, the reph that is typed after the syllable it belongs to, the vowel signs that legacy fonts draw as two separate glyphs, and the conjuncts क्ष, त्र, ज्ञ and श्र.
Your text stays on your machine

There is no server. The conversion engine is JavaScript that runs in your browser, so nothing you paste is uploaded, logged or stored. You can load the page, disconnect from the internet, and it will still work. For anyone handling draft orders, file notings or personal records, that is the point.
Where it is incomplete

Kruti Dev and Unicode are done and covered by tests. DevLys is seeded from the Kruti Dev layout and mostly works but has not been verified. Chanakya is not mapped at all yet, and the converter refuses that pair rather than guessing. Pages that are not finished are marked and kept out of search results.
English-word detection is a heuristic, not a certainty. A legacy font stores Hindi as plain ASCII, so there is no way to be perfect about it. Numbers, dates, URLs and email addresses are always safe.
